note: sin(7pi/14) = sin(pi/2) = 1, so the product reduces to sin(pi/14)sin(3pi/14)sin(5pi/14), the standard 1/8 identity. Numeric check at 40 dps gives 0.125000000..., matching B and separating it cleanly from 1/4 and sqrt(2)/7.

With A = ln x and B = ln y the expression is cos A cos B - (1/2)[cos(A-B) + cos(A+B)], and the bracket is exactly 2 cos A cos B, so the value is identically 0. Evaluated at four discriminating pairs (2,3), (5,0.7), (1.3,11), (0.4,0.25) it returns ~1e-41 while (1/2)f(x)f(y) and f(x+y) are far from zero there, so B and C are ruled out.

The condition gives tan(theta+alpha) = 1, so alpha = pi/4 - theta + n*pi. Then (1-tan alpha)/(1+tan alpha) = tan(pi/4 - alpha) = tan(theta). Verified at theta = 0.3, 1.1, -0.7, 2.4 for n = 0, 1, -1: the expression equals tan(theta) every time, and those points separate tan(theta) from -tan(theta), -cos(theta) and 0.

a sin t + b cos t = sqrt(a^2+b^2) sin(t + phi), so the maximum is sqrt(a^2+b^2). A fine scan over one period with (a,b) = (3,4) gives 5.0 and with (a,b) = (-2,5) gives 5.3852, against |a|+|b| = 7 in both cases, so option B (which is |a|+|b|) is excluded by the second, discriminating pair.

Putting s = sin^2 x gives s^4 + (1-s)^3 - 1 = s(s-1)(s^2+3), so on [0,1] only s = 0 and s = 1, i.e. sin x = 0 or cos x = 0, giving 5 points in the closed interval [0, 2pi]. Worth flagging: sympy's solveset returned only {0, pi/2, 3pi/2, 2pi} and silently dropped x = pi, which is a genuine solution (0 + (-1)^6 = 1); a 200k-point numeric scan finds all 5.

Clearing cos x gives 2 sin^2 x + sin x - 1 = 0, i.e. (2 sin x - 1)(sin x + 1) = 0. sin x = -1 gives x = 3pi/2, where cos x = 0 and both tan x and sec x are undefined, so it is rejected; sin x = 1/2 gives pi/6 and 5pi/6. A crude sign-change scan does flag 3pi/2 because sin x + 1 vanishes there too (a removable singularity of the combined quotient), but the stated function is undefined at that point.
cos 4x has period pi/2 and tan 3x has period pi/3; the LCM of pi/2 and pi/3 is pi. Tested numerically at five sample points: pi/12, pi/6 and pi/2 all fail as periods, pi holds to 1e-20.

sqrt(1-2x) needs x <= 1/2; the arcsine needs -1 <= (3x-1)/2 <= 1, i.e. -1/3 <= x <= 1. Intersection is [-1/3, 1/2]. Boundary checks confirm x = -0.4 fails the arcsine condition and x = 0.51 fails the radical, while both endpoints -1/3 and 1/2 are admissible.

2 arctan(1/2) has tan = (2*(1/2))/(1-1/4) = 4/3, so its cot is 3/4. With phi = arccos(3/4), sin phi = sqrt(7)/4 and sin 2phi = 2*(3/4)*(sqrt(7)/4) = 3 sqrt(7)/8. Direct 40 dps evaluation matches option A digit for digit; the other three options are 1.65, 6.61 and 3.97, all outside [-1,1] except B.
Slope = (a-4)/(-2-3) = (a-4)/(-5) = -2/5 gives a - 4 = 2, so a = 6. Solved symbolically for confirmation.

The collinearity determinant is 9pq - 3p - 3q = 0; dividing by -3pq gives 1/p + 1/q - 3 = 0. Checked at three discriminating collinear pairs (p,q) = (2, 2/5), (1/2, 1), (5/3, 5/12): 1/p + 1/q is 3 every time, while 1/p + 3/q takes the values 8, 5 and 39/5, so option D is not an identity.

If the intercepts are (A,0) and (0,B) then the midpoint (A/2, B/2) = (1,1) forces A = B = 2, so x/2 + y/2 = 1, i.e. x + y = 2. Confirmed the other way as well: only option D passes through both (2,0) and (0,2), and only its own intercept midpoint is (1,1) (A gives (3/4, 3/2), B gives (3/4, -3/2), C is a line through the origin with no proper intercept segment).

Slopes are -sqrt(3) and -1/sqrt(3); tan of the angle is |(m1-m2)/(1+m1 m2)| = (2/sqrt(3))/2 = 1/sqrt(3), so the acute angle is pi/6. Sympy simplifies the arctan to exactly pi/6. Note option C, 5pi/2, is not a valid angle between two lines at all.

p1 = |a|/sqrt(sec^2 t + cosec^2 t) = |a sin 2t|/2, so 4 p1^2 = a^2 sin^2 2t; and p2 = |a cos 2t| since the second line's normal is a unit vector, so p2^2 = a^2 cos^2 2t. The sum is a^2. Verified at five (theta, a) pairs (0.7,3), (1.3,2), (0.2,5), (2.9,1.5), (-0.5,4) where a^2, a and 1/a^2 all differ; the result equals a^2 in every case.
Eliminating theta gives (x-2)^2 + (y+1)^2 = 9 identically, so the centre is (2, -1). Confirmed symbolically.
